![Seven colonial audiencia sub-regions and 99 catalogued settlements across Mexico and Central America from 1518 to 1650.](figures/conquest_collapse_mesoamerica_regional_map.png)



# Abstract

Between the first Spanish landfalls on the Gulf littoral in 1518 and the demographic nadir of the mid-seventeenth century around 1650, Mexico and Central America suffered the steepest sustained population contraction recorded in early modern historical demography. Across seven colonial *audiencia* and frontier sub-regions spanning 2.595.905,5 km² from the northern arid marches of Nueva Vizcaya to the Isthmus of Panama, archival tributary reconstructions reconciled to the *Suma de Visitas* (1548 to 1550) and the *Relaciones Geográficas* (1577 to 1585) indicate a collapse from 18,17M inhabitants in 1518 to 6,54M in 1550 (−64%), 3,24M in 1600 (−82,2%) and 2,77M by 1650 (−84,7%) [@BorahCook1963; @Gerhard1993; @Whitmore1992]. Over the same seven polygons, JAGUAR's gridded spatial raster integration — constrained by centennial global substrata anchored near conservative contact baselines — tracks a parallel trough from 4,08M (4.077.678) in 1518 down to 2,25M (2.254.136, −44,7%) at 1600 before centennial interpolation toward 1700 lifts the 1650 frame to 2,99M (2.993.547, mean density 1,15 inhabitants per km²). Both frameworks converge closely across the seventeenth-century colonial floor (2,25M to 3,24M between 1600 and 1650), matching viceregal fiscal enumerations of 3.380.012 inhabitants for New Spain in 1570 and 1.712.615 in 1646 [@AguirreBeltran1946; @CookBorah1971]. Repeated virgin-soil epidemics — beginning with the 1520 smallpox *hueyzahuatl* and 1531 measles waves and culminating in the megadrought-amplified *cocoliztli* haemorrhagic and enteric outbreaks of 1545 to 1548 and 1576 to 1581, linked by ancient pathogen genomes to *Salmonella enterica* Paratyphi C — interacted with conquest warfare, *encomienda* tribute exactions, Isthmian Indian slaving and forced *congregaciones* to hollow out tropical lowlands by more than 90% while leaving denser surviving indigenous peasantries in the volcanic highlands of central Mexico, Oaxaca and Guatemala [@AcunaSoto2002; @Vagene2018; @Lovell1992; @Newson1986]. Simultaneously, a catalogued gazetteer of 99 settlements (rank-size $\alpha = 0,74$, $R^2 = 0,95$) exposes a sharp urban inversion: 43 pre-Columbian centres contracted dramatically (Tenochtitlan-Mexico City falling from 212k in 1519 to 48,6k in 1600 and 52,4k in 1646), while 56 newly planted Spanish cities, ports and silver camps — led by Puebla de los Ángeles (26,8k), Antigua Guatemala (24,5k) and Zacatecas (16,8k) — forged the enduring colonial urban spine.

# Background

## Contact-Era Demographic Geography and Historiographical Poles

When Spanish expeditions skirted the Yucatán coast in 1517 to 1518 and marched inland from Veracruz toward Tenochtitlan in 1519, they entered the most densely settled agricultural realm in the Western Hemisphere north of the central Andes. Intensive *chinampa* raised-field farming in the Basin of Mexico, terraced piedmont cultivation across Puebla-Tlaxcala, the Mixteca Alta and Lake Pátzcuaro, and irrigated valley plots in highland Guatemala and Pacific Nicaragua sustained a dense patchwork of tributary states and urban *altepetl* [@BorahCook1963; @Gerhard1993; @Lovell1992]. Yet no single number in American historical demography has provoked fiercer controversy than the size of that contact-era population on the eve of 1519.

For more than seven decades, scholarship has polarised between high-counter and low-counter schools. At the upper bound, Woodrow Borah and Sherburne F. Cook combined the 1519 *Matrícula de Tributos* with backward extrapolation from mid-sixteenth-century *visitas* to estimate 25,2M inhabitants for Central Mexico alone in 1519, implying a loss exceeding 95% by 1605 [@BorahCook1963; @CookBorah1971]. At the lower extreme, Ángel Rosenblat and later minimalist critics argued for roughly 4,5M across all of Mexico, while Francis J. Brooks challenged the demographic scale of the 1520 smallpox epidemic by questioning whether sixteenth-century Franciscan chroniclers inflated native death tolls [@Brooks1993].

Between those extremes, modern historical geography and stochastic simulation have converged on a formidable, though somewhat less extreme, catastrophic consensus. Using multi-disease demographic micro-simulation anchored to Basin of Mexico archaeological settlement surveys and tributary censuses, Thomas M. Whitmore placed contact-era Central Mexico near 16M (and the Basin of Mexico at roughly 1,59M falling to 175k by 1607, an 89% contraction) [@Whitmore1992]. Robert McCaa answered Brooks's scepticism directly through non-quantitative historical demography — cross-checking Nahuatl annals, Spanish legal testimonies, *encomienda* vacancy petitions and clerical laments — to demonstrate that even if exact contact totals remain uncertain within a factor of two, sixteenth-century Mexico indisputably suffered a demographic catastrophe rather than a gentle decline [@Mccaa1999Siglo]. Parallel regional syntheses for Central America by Murdo J. MacLeod, W. George Lovell and Linda A. Newson reached congruent findings: Guatemala, Chiapas and San Salvador held over 2M inhabitants at contact, while Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama together supported roughly 2,3M to 2,4M before epidemic waves and slaving reduced the isthmus to a fraction of its former density [@MacLeod1973; @Lovell1989Supervivientes; @Newson1986].

## Virgin-Soil Epidemics and the Cocoliztli-Megadrought Synergy

The biological engine of collapse was the abrupt reunification of Old and New World disease pools after millennia of oceanic isolation [@Guillermoherrera2021Epidemias; @Whitmore1992]. Mesoamerican populations lacked acquired immunity to Eurasian acute crowd infections, and because dense urban corridors linked highland basins to coastal ports along royal highways and tribute routes, pathogens travelled faster than Spanish armies. The opening blow arrived in the spring of 1520, when an infected African soldier in Pánfilo de Narváez's expedition carried smallpox (*hueyzahuatl*, the great rash) ashore at Veracruz. Sweeping across Cempoala, Tlaxcala and besieged Tenochtitlan between May and November 1520, smallpox killed Mexica ruler Cuitláhuac, crippled urban provisioning and struck down an estimated one-quarter to two-fifths of exposed highland communities in a single season [@Guillermoherrera2021Epidemias; @Mccaa1999Siglo]. Smallpox raced southward along indigenous trade arteries into Guatemala and Nicaragua years before Pedro de Alvarado's columns reached the Kaqchikel and K'iche' highlands in 1524 [@Lovell1989Supervivientes; @MacLeod1973].

Recovery was repeatedly truncated before a single generation could replace its dead. Measles (*tepiton zahuatl*) struck New Spain and Guatemala in 1531 to 1532, followed by influenza, mumps and pneumonic plagues across the 1530s [@Guillermoherrera2021Epidemias; @Lovell1992]. Even deadlier were the two great sixteenth-century *cocoliztli* ("pestilence") pandemics of 1545 to 1548 and 1576 to 1581. Contemporary Spanish physicians such as Francisco Hernández and Nahua chroniclers recorded high fever, severe headache, vertigo, dysentery and profuse bleeding from the nose, mouth and eyes that killed victims within three to five days [@Malanga2020Earth; @Varella2022Peste]. Tree-ring chronologies compiled by Rodolfo Acuña-Soto and colleagues revealed that both *cocoliztli* outbreaks coincided with two of the severest multi-year megadroughts in North America over the past half-millennium, provoking crop failures, famine-driven migration and acute water contamination [@AcunaSoto2002].

Recent palaeogenomics has sharpened the biological diagnosis of *cocoliztli*. Ancient DNA extracted from teeth in the 1545 to 1550 epidemic cemetery at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in the Mixteca Alta of Oaxaca identified *Salmonella enterica* subsp. *enterica* serovar Paratyphi C — a lethal enteric fever pathogen carried from Europe — directly in the pulp chambers of epidemic victims [@Vagene2018]. Enteric fever thrived under the very ecological conditions documented by colonial observers: drought-shrunken water sources, crowded colonial resettlement towns, inadequate human waste disposal (whose wider epidemiological weight in Maya and Mesoamerican settlements has also been emphasised in sanitation studies [@Alfred2017Impact]) and abrupt changes in indigenous clothing and shelter during colonial restructuring [@Carabes2021Changes]. Whether Paratyphi C acted alone or alongside rodent-borne haemorrhagic fever amplified by drought-rain anomalies, the demographic toll was staggering: the 1545 to 1548 outbreak erased an estimated 40% to 50% of the surviving indigenous population, and the 1576 to 1581 visitation cut the remaining tributary rolls nearly in half once more [@CookBorah1971; @AcunaSoto2002; @Guillermoherrera2021Epidemias]. Subsequent outbreaks of typhus (*matlazáhuatl*), measles and smallpox in 1588, 1595, 1615 and 1631 prevented any sustained rebound until after 1650, while recurrent generational smallpox cycles continued to scar highland Guatemala and Yucatán for centuries thereafter [@Lovell2021Destroying; @Moguel2024Primera].

## Lowland Collapse, Highland Survival and Colonial Institutions

Mortality was never geographically uniform. Across Mexico and Central America, elevation drew the sharpest epidemiological boundary of the colonial era [@Gerhard1993; @Newson1986; @MacLeod1973]. Along the hot, humid *tierra caliente* lowlands — Veracruz, Pánuco, Tabasco, coastal Oaxaca, Soconusco, the Caribbean and Pacific coasts of Honduras and Nicaragua, and the Isthmus of Panama — indigenous populations fell by 90% to 98% within two generations. Introduced *Plasmodium* malaria and later yellow fever established permanent tropical reservoirs alongside smallpox and enteric disease, turning once-populous coastal provinces such as Pánuco (whose head town plunged from 9,75k in 1519 to 1,28k in 1646) and lowland Panama into thinly peopled cattle savannas and timber backwaters [@Gerhard1993; @Newson1986]. By contrast, cool *tierra fría* and *tierra templada* highland valleys above 1.500 m — the Basin of Mexico, Puebla-Tlaxcala, the Valley of Toluca, Michoacán, the Mixteca Alta, Chiapas and the Guatemalan Cuchumatanes — escaped endemic malaria and retained substantial indigenous majorities despite losing 75% to 88% of their pre-contact headcount [@Lovell1992; @Whitmore1992].

Disease never operated in a vacuum; colonial political economy magnified every epidemic shock [@Varella2022Peste; @Mccaa1999Siglo]. Sixteenth-century clerical factions debating the causes of Indian mortality explicitly linked *encomienda* tribute quotas, *repartimiento* labour drafts and forced porterage (*tamemes*) to physiological exhaustion and impaired household recovery [@Varella2022Peste]. In Nicaragua and Honduras during the 1520s and 1530s, Spanish conquistadors exported tens of thousands of enslaved indigenous captives through El Realejo and Trujillo to Peru and Panama, stripping Pacific Nicaragua of its demographic core even faster than disease alone could accomplish [@MacLeod1973; @Newson1986]. Across central New Spain, the collapse of indigenous tillage opened vast tracts of vacated valley land to Spanish wheat estates and multiplying herds of sheep, cattle and horses, a rural ecological revolution documented parish by parish in the 1577 to 1585 *Relaciones Geográficas* [@Montemayor2024Geographical].

To arrest fiscal erosion and consolidate parish evangelisation, Crown and Church pushed two waves of forced nucleated resettlement (*congregaciones* or *reducciones*), first in the 1550s under missionary leadership and then systematically across central Mexico between 1598 and 1605 following the Third Mexican Provincial Council of 1585 [@Salvador2013Clero; @Gerhard1993]. Herding dispersed hamlet survivors into grid-plan colonial towns simplified tribute collection and catechesis, yet it simultaneously increased crowd-disease transmission and severed rural communities from dispersed upland plots, deepening Nahua cultural dislocation and demographic fragility [@Malanga2020Earth; @Salvador2013Clero]. Meanwhile, the discovery of rich silver lodes at Taxco, Pachuca, Guanajuato (1548 to 1554), Zacatecas (1546) and San Luis Potosí (1592) pulled multi-ethnic streams of free wage-earning *naborías*, Tlaxcalan colonists, Spanish miners and enslaved Africans northward into the Chichimeca frontier of Nueva Galicia and Nueva Vizcaya [@Gerhard1993; @Galindo2023Forms; @AguirreBeltran1946]. By 1646, New Spain's demographic profile had been permanently transformed: indigenous communities stood at their historic nadir, while Spaniards, *mestizos*, enslaved and free Afro-Mexicans (numbering well over 150k by mid-century [@AguirreBeltran1946]) and even several thousand Asian *chinos* arriving aboard the Manila Galleon through Acapulco had begun to populate the cities, ports and mining *reales* [@Slack2012Orientalizing].

# Methodology

## Colonial Audiencia Partition and Dual-Series Architecture

To track epidemic collapse and colonial resettlement across coherent administrative and ecological units rather than anachronistic modern borders, JAGUAR partitions mainland Mexico and Central America into seven colonial *audiencia* and frontier sub-regions covering 2.595.905,5 km² (31.729 grid cells at 5 arc-minute resolution; Figure \ref{fig:hero-conquest-map}). Boundary polygons derive from sixteenth- and seventeenth-century HGIS de las Indias *audiencia* and *gobernación* frameworks paired with OpenHistoricalMap frontier geometries and HydroBASINS watersheds along the Caribbean Mosquitia littoral.

The seven sub-regions capture distinct ecological and institutional trajectories. First, the Audiencia de Mexico Central Core (452.616 km²) encompasses the Basin of Mexico, Puebla-Tlaxcala, Michoacán, Oaxaca, Morelos, Guerrero and the Veracruz-Pánuco Gulf corridor. Second, the Audiencia de Nueva Galicia and West Mexico (197.949,3 km²) spans Guadalajara, the Bajío margin, Colima-Jalisco and the southern Zacatecas silver belt. Third, Yucatan and Tabasco (152.646 km²) covers the karst Maya lowlands of Mérida and Campeche together with the fluvial swamps of Tabasco. Fourth, Nueva Vizcaya and the Northern Mining Frontier (1.143.822,7 km², 44,1% of the chapter's land area) stretches across Durango, Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León, Sonora, Sinaloa and Baja California. Fifth, the Audiencia de Guatemala, Chiapas and San Salvador (251.067,8 km²) binds the highland Maya heartland to the Pacific cacao belt of Soconusco and Izalcos. Sixth, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica (310.747,3 km²) unites the Pacific lake corridor, central silver highlands and humid Caribbean slopes. Seventh, Tierra Firme — the Audiencia de Panama and Veraguas (87.056,4 km²) — anchors the trans-isthmian corridor linking Panamá Viejo to Nombre de Dios and Portobelo.

A decisive methodological feature of the 1518 to 1650 epoch is the tension between global centennial spatial rasters and fine-grained archival tributary counts. Rather than concealing that discrepancy, this chapter presents and reconciles two explicit series across the identical seven-region mask. The first is the gridded spatial raster integration (the chapter spatial summary), computed directly by summing JAGUAR's 5-arc-minute population rasters inside each sub-regional polygon at the centennial frames of 1500, 1600 and 1700 and log-linearly interpolating the domain endpoints at 1518 and 1650:

$$P_r^{\text{grid}}(t) = \sum_{c \in \Omega_r} \rho_c(t), \qquad P_r^{\text{grid}}(t) = \exp\!\left[(1 - \lambda)\ln P_r^{\text{grid}}(t_0) + \lambda \ln P_r^{\text{grid}}(t_1)\right]$$

where $\Omega_r$ denotes the set of masked grid cells belonging to sub-region $r$, $\rho_c(t)$ is the raster headcount in cell $c$, and $\lambda = (t - t_0)/(t_1 - t_0)$ for any non-centennial year $t \in (t_0, t_1)$.

The second series is the archival ethnohistorical benchmark ledger, reconstructed directly from sixteenth- and seventeenth-century tributary rolls (*Suma de Visitas* 1548 to 1550, *Relaciones Geográficas* 1577 to 1585, López de Velasco 1574, Vázquez de Espinosa 1628 and bishopric counts of 1646) reconciled against regional syntheses by Borah and Cook, Gerhard, Whitmore, Lovell, MacLeod and Newson [@BorahCook1963; @CookBorah1971; @Gerhard1993; @Whitmore1992; @Lovell1992; @MacLeod1973; @Newson1986]. Tributary totals $T_r(t)$ are converted to total indigenous population using period-specific demographic multipliers $k(t)$ that reflect changing household size and widow/minor exemption rules:

$$P_r^{\text{arch}}(t) = k(t) \cdot T_r(t) + P_r^{\text{non-ind}}(t)$$

Following Cook, Borah and Gerhard, $k(t)$ declines from approximately 3,3 to 3,5 persons per full tributary during the 1548 *Suma de Visitas* (when many *macehuales* and *mayeques* remained exempt or uncounted) toward 2,8 to 3 after the uniform head-tax reforms of the 1560s, while $P_r^{\text{non-ind}}(t)$ adds Spanish, *mestizo*, Afro-Mexican and Asian urban and mining residents documented in colonial censuses [@CookBorah1971; @Gerhard1993; @AguirreBeltran1946; @Slack2012Orientalizing].

## Settlement Gazetteer Compilation and Rank-Size Scaling

Urban and regional central-place trajectories were assembled across four sequential ingestion waves tracked in the chapter source ledger, yielding 99 catalogued settlements across all seven sub-regions and seven modern countries (Mexico 68, Panama 9, Guatemala 6, Honduras 5, Nicaragua 4, El Salvador 4 and Costa Rica 3) with 0% crowd-sourced fallback share. Wave 1 primary archival and census ingestion supplied 91 settlements (91,92%), drawing upon the *Suma de Visitas*, *Relaciones Geográficas*, López de Velasco, Vázquez de Espinosa and HGIS de las Indias colonial registers. Wave 2 peer-reviewed demographic monographs added six regional towns (+6,59% marginal gain), Wave 3 longitudinal backfill added one (+1,03%) and Wave 4 gap-hunter verification added one (+1,02%), confirming saturation across every sub-region (Audiencia de Mexico 33, Guatemala-Chiapas-San Salvador 13, Nueva Vizcaya 12, Honduras-Nicaragua-Costa Rica 12, Nueva Galicia 10, Yucatán-Tabasco 10 and Tierra Firme 9).

Every entry is standardised to city-proper boundaries (99 city-proper settlements, 0 suburbs) to avoid double-counting tributary *sujetos* around indigenous *cabeceras* or rural *haciendas* around Spanish towns. Urban hierarchy scaling is evaluated by ordinary least-squares log-log regression over the leading 49 settlements out of the full 99-settlement sample:

$$\log_{10} P_{(i)} = \beta_0 - \alpha \log_{10}(i)$$

where $P_{(i)}$ denotes the peak recorded population of the settlement at rank $i$ and $\alpha$ measures hierarchical concentration relative to the Zipf benchmark ($\alpha = 1$).

# Testing and Validation

## Reconciling Gridded Centennial Substrata with Archival Benchmarks

Comparing JAGUAR's gridded raster integration against the archival ethnohistorical benchmark series across all seven sub-regions exposes the exact mathematical source of divergence at contact and the striking convergence by the seventeenth-century nadir (Table \ref{tab:dual-reconciliation}). At 1518, the archival series places Mexico and Central America at 18,17M inhabitants (a moderate catastrophic consensus sitting comfortably below Borah and Cook's 25,2M Central Mexico ceiling yet well above minimalist estimates), whereas the gridded raster integration registers 4,08M (4.077.678). That 4,46-fold gap at contact arises directly from global centennial raster calibration, which aligns 1500 pre-contact New World density toward conservative low-counter totals and lacks sub-centennial frames to resolve the 1519 to 1548 freefall.

Once the sixteenth-century epidemic waves subside into the colonial trough, however, both reconstructions tighten into remarkable alignment. At 1600, archival totals stand at 3,24M against 2,25M in the gridded raster (ratio 1,44); by 1650, archival totals bottom out at 2,77M against 2,99M in the gridded raster (ratio 0,93 — within 7,4%!). Notice too why the gridded curve turns upward between 1600 and 1650 while the archival curve edges downward from 3,24M to 2,77M: because the gridded raster interpolates log-linearly between the 1600 trough and the 1700 colonial recovery raster, it cannot capture the late-nadir dip of 1620 to 1646 caused by the 1595, 1615 and 1631 outbreaks and the dislocation of the 1598 to 1605 *congregaciones* [@Gerhard1993; @Whitmore1992; @Salvador2013Clero]. For 1518 to 1650 demographic dynamics, therefore, the archival series tracks epidemic timing more faithfully, whereas the gridded series anchors continuous spatial mass conservation into the eighteenth-century recovery.

## Cross-Checks Against Scraped Colonial HGIS Enumerations

Independent external validation comes from authentic colonial fiscal and provincial enumerations extracted from HGIS de las Indias, OpenHistoricalMap historical boundary ledgers and Gonzalo Aguirre Beltrán and Peter Gerhard's viceregal aggregates (Table \ref{tab:hgis-subadmin}). These primary administrative series bracket our 1570 to 1650 colonial floor directly and provide a clean continuity hinge to the 1700 provincial recovery.

Every major administrative benchmark aligns tightly with our chapter reconstructions. Aguirre Beltrán and Gerhard's viceregal total for colonial New Spain falls from 3.380.012 inhabitants in 1570 (just before the 1576 *cocoliztli* catastrophe) to 1.712.615 in 1646 — a 49,3% drop over seventy-six years that closely mirrors our four Mexican sub-regions' archival decline from roughly 2,48M in 1600 to 2,1M in 1650 (and gridded range of 1,77M in 1600 to 2,32M in 1650) once peripheral northern frontier groups outside royal fiscal rolls are included [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Gerhard1993]. At the *audiencia* level in 1600, HGIS de las Indias assigns 1.550.000 inhabitants to the Audiencia de Mexico, 460.000 to the Audiencia de Guatemala, Chiapas, Petén and San Salvador, 270.000 to Nueva Vizcaya and the northern frontier, 260.000 to Nueva Galicia and 215.000 to Yucatán and Tabasco — matching our sub-regional archival series almost figure for figure.

# Results

## Macro-Regional Trajectory and the Gridded Spatial Curve (1518 to 1650)

Across Mexico and Central America, demographic contraction unfolded in two steep epidemiological steps followed by a prolonged, geographically uneven trough (Figure \ref{fig:conquest-trajectory}). In the archival benchmark series, aggregate population plunged by 11,64M (−64%) in just thirty-two years between 1518 (18,17M) and 1550 (6,54M) under the combined weight of the 1520 smallpox pandemic, conquest violence, the 1531 to 1532 measles outbreak, Isthmian slaving and the first *cocoliztli* disaster of 1545 to 1548 [@BorahCook1963; @AcunaSoto2002; @Vagene2018]. Over the next half-century to 1600, the 1576 to 1581 *cocoliztli* pandemic and subsequent typhus and measles visitations halved the surviving population once again, reducing the chapter total to 3,24M (−82,2% below 1518). Between 1600 and 1650, the rate of loss finally slowed (−14,4% over fifty years), settling at an archival nadir of 2,77M inhabitants (1,07 inhabitants per km² across 2,6M km²), roughly one-seventh of the pre-contact population.

## Central New Spain: The Audiencia de Mexico Core

Despite enduring the fiercest epidemiological assaults of the sixteenth century, the Audiencia de Mexico Central Core (452.616 km²) remained the demographic fulcrum of Mesoamerica throughout the entire era. In 1518, its archival total of 10,2M accounted for 56,1% of the chapter's population (density 22,5 inhabitants per km² across highlands and coasts combined, exceeding 100 inhabitants per km² inside the Basin of Mexico). By 1550, after the 1520 smallpox siege, the 1531 measles wave and the 1545 to 1548 *cocoliztli* epidemic, that base had fallen by 64,2% to 3,65M [@BorahCook1963; @CookBorah1971; @Carabes2021Changes]. The 1576 to 1581 *cocoliztli* disaster and the 1598 to 1605 *congregaciones* cut the region further to 1,55M by 1600 and 1,22M by 1650 (−88% below 1518) [@Gerhard1993; @Salvador2013Clero; @Whitmore1992]. Gridded integration traces a parallel concentration: falling from 1,55M in 1518 to 1,12M in 1600 (−27,9%) and recovering modestly to 1,2M by 1650, the Central Core still commanded 40% of the gridded chapter population and easily its highest 1650 density at 2,65 inhabitants per km² (Panel B of Figure \ref{fig:conquest-trajectory}).

Internally, however, the Central Core split sharply by elevation. Along the Gulf coast of Veracruz and Pánuco, indigenous villages vanished almost entirely; Pánuco dropped from 9,75k in 1519 to 1,28k in 1646 (−86,9%), while the Spanish port of Veracruz — relocated repeatedly to escape yellow fever and *vómito negro* — grew only to 6,2k by 1646, reliant on enslaved African dockworkers and muleteers [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Gerhard1993]. In the highland valleys, ancient *altepetl* lost three-quarters of their people yet endured as structured indigenous municipalities: Cholula fell from 36,8k to 8,2k (−77,7%), Tlaxcala from 31,4k to 7,6k (−75,8%), Huejotzingo from 24,9k to 5,2k (−79,1%), Texcoco from 24,8k to 5,8k (−76,6%) and Xochimilco from 23,4k to 5,4k (−76,9%) [@Malanga2020Earth; @Montemayor2024Geographical]. In Michoacán, the Purépecha royal seat of Tzintzuntzan collapsed by 90,8% (31,9k to 2,95k) as Bishop Vasco de Quiroga moved the cathedral to Pátzcuaro (which peaked at 14,2k in 1548 before easing to 5,4k) and the Crown later promoted Spanish Valladolid Michoacán (rising from 1,45k in 1545 to 7,2k in 1646). In the Mixteca Alta of Oaxaca — epicentre of the genetically confirmed *Salmonella enterica* Paratyphi C mass grave at Teposcolula — Yanhuitlán fell from 13,8k to 3,45k and Teposcolula from 11,9k to 3,15k, even as the Spanish valley capital of Antequera de Oaxaca rose from 2,4k in 1532 to 9,4k in 1646 [@Vagene2018; @Gerhard1993]. Most strikingly of all, the brand-new Spanish city of Puebla de los Ángeles — laid out in 1531 between Cholula and Tlaxcala to house Spanish artisans and wheat farmers — expanded fourteenfold from 1,85k in 1534 to 26,8k by 1646, overtaking every indigenous city outside Mexico City itself.

## Western Silver Corridors and the Northern Frontier

North and west of the Tarascan and Otomí marches, Spanish colonisation reversed the pre-contact gradient of empty drylands and crowded southern valleys. In the Audiencia de Nueva Galicia and West Mexico (197.949,3 km²), Nuño de Guzmán's brutal 1530 to 1531 campaign, the Mixtón War of 1540 to 1542 and successive epidemics drove archival totals from 1,45M in 1518 down to 520k in 1550 and 260k in 1600 (−82,1%), matched by a 52,5% gridded contraction from 431k to 204,9k [@Gerhard1993]. Yet Nueva Galicia became the single earliest sub-region in New Spain to rebound in archival records, climbing back from 260k in 1600 to 285k by 1650 (and 299k gridded, density 1,51 inhabitants per km²). Silver fuelled that turnaround. Following the 1546 strike at Cerro de la Bufa, Zacatecas swelled from 4,2k in 1550 to 14,6k in 1605 and 16,8k by 1646, becoming the third-largest Spanish-dominated city in Mexico; Guadalajara expanded more than fivefold from 2,15k in 1548 to 11,4k in 1646 as the judicial and commercial pivot of the west, while secondary Bajío and silver hubs — Guanajuato (8,4k), Querétaro (10,4k), Celaya, Lagos de Moreno, Aguascalientes, Sombrerete and Fresnillo — knitted together an integrated agro-mining economy supplying wheat, maize, hides and tallow to the silver camps [@Gerhard1993; @Montemayor2024Geographical].

Farther north lay the vast expanse of Nueva Vizcaya and the Northern Mining Frontier (1.143.822,7 km²), spanning 44,1% of the chapter's territory yet holding its lowest 1650 density at 0,47 inhabitants per km². Semi-sedentary and mobile Chichimeca, Tepehuán, Tarahumara, Yaqui and Mayo peoples suffered severe disruption from Spanish slaving raids, mission *reducciones* and the bitter Chichimeca War (1550 to 1590), pulling archival numbers from 950k in 1518 to 440k in 1600 and 380k in 1650 (−60%, a noticeably gentler proportional fall than central Mesoamerica because dispersed settlement slowed crowd-disease cascades, though gridded estimates register a sharper 67% dip from 827,1k in 1518 to 272,7k in 1600 before rebounding to 542k in 1650) [@Galindo2023Forms; @Gerhard1993]. After peace treaties settled Tlaxcalan colonist families alongside northern mines and missions during the 1590s, a sparse urban archipelago anchored royal control across the arid plateau: San Luis Potosí jumped from 3,8k in 1595 to 9,4k in 1646, Hidalgo del Parral surged after its 1631 silver strike, and Durango, Saltillo, Monterrey, Culiacán, Santa Bárbara and Sinaloa de Leyva established permanent northern administrative nodes relying on coerced mission labour, debt peonage and free indigenous migrants [@Galindo2023Forms].

## Yucatán, Tabasco and the Maya Heartland

Across Yucatan and Tabasco (152.646 km²), demographic collapse followed a protracted military and ecological curve. Tabasco's low-lying Grijalva-Usumacinta delta suffered immediate epidemic devastation after 1519, while the protracted Montejo campaigns across the limestone Yucatán peninsula (1527 to 1546) coincided with famine, forced *congregaciones* and Franciscan parish reorganisation [@Gerhard1993; @Salvador2013Clero]. Archival headcounts fell from 950k in 1518 to 340k in 1550, 225k in 1600 and 210k by 1650 (−77,9%), while gridded integration falls by 68,2% from 535,8k in 1518 to 170,2k in 1600 before reaching 281,9k in 1650 (1,85 inhabitants per km², second densest among all seven sub-regions). Unlike the heavily depopulated Gulf littoral of Veracruz, northwestern Yucatán retained a resilient Yucatec Maya peasantry clustered around *encomienda* towns such as Maní, Izamal, Motul and Tekax, anchored by Spanish Mérida (rising from 4,2k in 1545 to 12,6k in 1646), the fortified Gulf port of Campeche and inland Valladolid Yucatán, whereas eastern frontier outposts such as Bacalar withered under Maya flight into the unconquered Petén forest and pirate raids [@Alfred2017Impact; @Moguel2024Primera].

## Central America: Guatemala Highlands, Isthmian Collapse and Panama

South of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, the three Central American sub-regions exhibited the hemisphere's starkest contrast between highland endurance and lowland annihilation [@MacLeod1973; @Lovell1989Supervivientes; @Newson1986]. In the Audiencia de Guatemala, Chiapas and San Salvador (251.067,8 km²), pre-conquest K'iche', Kaqchikel, Mam, Tzotzil and Pipil polities supported an archival population of 2,25M in 1518. Pre-invasion smallpox (1519 to 1521), Pedro de Alvarado's conquest campaigns, the 1545 to 1548 *gucumatz* (*cocoliztli*) plague and the 1576 to 1577 pandemic cut the sub-region to 820k in 1550, 460k in 1600 and 410k by 1650 (−81,8%; gridded series 247,5k in 1518 to 150,1k in 1600 and 257,7k in 1650, density 1,03 inhabitants per km²) [@Lovell1992; @Lovell1989Supervivientes]. Even so, highland Maya communities in Quetzaltenango, Totonicapán, Huehuetenango, Cobán (where Dominican *reducciones* consolidated Q'eqchi' settlements to 7,1k by 1646) and Chiapa de Corzo survived in sufficient numbers to sustain the Spanish capital of Santiago de Guatemala (Antigua Guatemala), which grew more than fivefold from 4,8k in 1545 to 24,5k by 1646 alongside San Salvador (9,2k) and the cacao boom town of Sonsonate (5,6k) [@MacLeod1973; @Lovell1992].

Far harsher was the fate of Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica (310.747,3 km²). From an archival contact total of 1,65M in 1518, the combined onslaught of Pedrarias Dávila's slave exports from Pacific Nicaragua (perhaps 200k to 400k captives shipped southward before 1550), gold-panning exhaustion in Olancho and virgin-soil epidemics slashed population by 74,5% in barely thirty years to 420k in 1550, plunging further to 210k in 1600 and 185k by 1650 (−88,8%; gridded series 386,7k in 1518 to 266,3k in 1600 and 328,4k in 1650, density 1,06 inhabitants per km²) [@Newson1986; @MacLeod1973]. Chorotega and Nicarao towns such as Masaya (9,6k in 1524 to 4,85k in 1646) and Nicoya shrank rapidly, leaving tiny Spanish villas — Granada, León Nicaragua, Comayagua, Tegucigalpa, Cartago Costa Rica and the Pacific shipyard of El Realejo — scattered across a largely emptied ranching and indigo landscape, while eastern Caribbean Mosquitia remained outside Spanish fiscal reach [@Newson1986].

At the southeastern terminus, Tierra Firme — the Audiencia de Panama and Veraguas (87.056,4 km²) — suffered the earliest and most thorough demographic erasure on the American mainland. Struck directly from 1514 onward by Balboa and Pedrarias Dávila's *entradas* out of Darién, indigenous Cueva and Guaymí societies collapsed from 720k in 1518 to 165k in 1550, 95k in 1600 and 82k by 1650 (−88,6%; gridded series 98,3k in 1518 to 71,4k in 1600 and 87,5k in 1650, density 1,01 inhabitants per km²) [@MacLeod1973; @Newson1986]. By 1600, Panama's demographic weight had shifted almost entirely onto the imperial silver-transit axis linking Panamá Viejo (10,8k in 1646) to Portobelo (which replaced unhealthy Nombre de Dios in 1597), sustained by enslaved and free African labourers, mule-train operators and modest ranching villas at Natá de los Caballeros, La Villa de Los Santos, Alanje and Santiago de Veraguas.

## Urban Hierarchy Inversion and Rank-Size Structure

Nothing illustrates the structural break between pre-Columbian Mesoamerica and early colonial New Spain more sharply than the diverging fortunes of the chapter's 99 catalogued settlements (Figure \ref{fig:conquest-hierarchy} and Table \ref{tab:top20-settlements}). Across the full 99-settlement distribution, peak recorded populations follow a moderately steep power-law rank-size curve ($\alpha = 0,74$, $R^2 = 0,95$ over the leading 49 settlements), lying well below classic imperial primacy ($\alpha \approx 1$) on the middle slope because a broad tier of provincial Spanish capitals and surviving highland *cabeceras* (9k to 37k) sat beneath a strongly primate capital. Yet that static peak curve masks a dramatic longitudinal inversion: 43 settlements contracted between their earliest and latest recorded benchmarks — virtually all of them indigenous pre-contact towns — whereas 56 settlements expanded, virtually all of them post-1519 Spanish foundations.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:conquest-hierarchy">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_jaguar/1.0-conquest-collapse-mesoamerica/conquest_collapse_mesoamerica_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:conquest-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Twelve largest catalogued settlements by peak population (Panel A) and log-log rank-size distribution across 99 settlements fitted over the leading 49 centres ($\alpha = 0,74$, $R^2 = 0,95$, Panel B), 1518 to 1650.</figcaption>
</figure>

In 1519, the 21 indigenous cities recorded at contact aggregated 549,6k urban residents, led overwhelmingly by Tenochtitlan (212k) and a dense highland constellation of Cholula (36,8k), Tzintzuntzan (31,9k), Tlaxcala (31,4k), Huejotzingo (24,9k), Texcoco (24,8k) and Xochimilco (23,4k). By 1646, across 97 settlements with mid-seventeenth-century counts, total catalogued urban population stood at 512,9k — nearly as large in aggregate as the 1519 contact core, yet completely reconfigured in geography and ethnic composition. Ciudad de México still stood first at 52,4k (having touched bottom at 48,6k around 1600), now flanked not by lakeside Nahua partners but by Spanish-founded Puebla de los Ángeles (26,8k), Antigua Guatemala (24,5k), Zacatecas (16,8k), Mérida (12,6k), Guadalajara (11,4k), Panamá Viejo (10,8k), Querétaro (10,4k), Antequera de Oaxaca (9,4k), San Luis Potosí (9,4k) and San Salvador (9,2k) [@Gerhard1993; @MacLeod1973; @AguirreBeltran1946; @Slack2012Orientalizing].

# Limitations

Five structural constraints bound demographic reconstruction across Mexico and Central America between 1518 and 1650.

First, contact-era population size in 1518 to 1519 carries the widest uncertainty interval of any epoch in the historical record. Because the earliest surviving systematic Spanish headcounts (*Suma de Visitas*, 1548 to 1550) post-date three decades of smallpox, measles, warfare and the first *cocoliztli* pandemic, backward projection to 1518 depends heavily on assumed tributary conversion multipliers and archaeological carrying-capacity bounds [@BorahCook1963; @Brooks1993; @Mccaa1999Siglo; @Whitmore1992]. Consequently, JAGUAR explicitly brackets our 18,17M archival baseline against the conservative 4,08M centennial raster integration, noting that true regional uncertainty around 1518 spans at least $\pm 35\%$ even within the moderate-catastrophe school, narrowing sharply to $\pm 15\%$ by 1600 to 1650.

Second, temporal sampling gaps in centennial global rasters (available at 1500, 1600 and 1700) cannot capture sub-centennial epidemic turning points. Log-linear interpolation between 1600 and 1700 produces an apparent gridded rise from 2,25M to 2,99M by 1650, masking the actual archival trough of 1620 to 1646 visible in bishopric counts and Aguirre Beltrán's 1646 New Spain aggregate (1.712.615) [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Gerhard1993]. Readers analysing short-run epidemic mortality between 1519 and 1646 should therefore rely on the archival and settlement series rather than interpolated centennial rasters.

Third, fiscal evasion and institutional shifts introduce systematic under-enumeration in sixteenth-century Spanish tribute rolls. Exempt indigenous nobles (*principales*), untaxed serfs (*mayeques*), widowed households, migrants fleeing *congregaciones* and communities retreating into unconquered forest or sierra refuges (the Petén Maya lowlands, Lacandón forest, Mosquitia, Darién and northern Chichimeca zones) escaped royal *tasaciones* to varying degrees, meaning post-1560 fiscal declines partially blend true excess mortality with flight and fiscal concealment [@CookBorah1971; @Salvador2013Clero; @Newson1986].

Fourth, multi-ethnic urban growth in Spanish cities and mining camps is unevenly documented relative to indigenous tributary towns. Early Spanish censuses counted *vecinos* (Spanish male householders) rather than total residents, often omitting indigenous *naborías*, enslaved and free Afro-Mexicans, *mestizos* and Pacific-rim Asian *chinos* unless separate parish or Inquisition records survive [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Slack2012Orientalizing; @Galindo2023Forms].

Fifth, biological attribution of individual sixteenth-century epidemics remains only partially resolved by palaeogenomics. While ancient DNA confirms *Salmonella enterica* Paratyphi C in the 1545 to 1550 Teposcolula-Yucundaa burial ground [@Vagene2018], co-circulating viral haemorrhagic fevers, typhus and dysentery may have acted synergistically during both the 1545 to 1548 and 1576 to 1581 megadroughts [@AcunaSoto2002; @Carabes2021Changes; @Guillermoherrera2021Epidemias].

# Conclusion

Between 1518 and 1650, Mexico and Central America experienced a demographic rupture without parallel in the early modern Atlantic world. Reconciling colonial tributary registers, *Relaciones Geográficas*, archaeological baselines and palaeogenomic evidence confirms that successive waves of smallpox, measles, typhus and megadrought-amplified *cocoliztli* — compounded by conquest disruption, *encomienda* extraction, Isthmian slaving and forced *congregaciones* — reduced the region's archival population by roughly 84,7%, from 18,17M in 1518 to 6,54M in 1550, 3,24M in 1600 and a nadir of 2,77M around 1650 [@BorahCook1963; @Whitmore1992; @AcunaSoto2002; @Vagene2018]. Gridded spatial raster integration registers the same colonial trough closely (2,25M in 1600 and 2,99M in 1650 across 2,6M km²), converging with viceregal fiscal benchmarks of 3,38M for New Spain in 1570 and 1,71M in 1646 [@AguirreBeltran1946; @Gerhard1993].

Out of that catastrophe emerged the durable spatial skeleton of colonial Mesoamerica. Tropical lowlands along the Gulf of Mexico, Pacific Nicaragua and Panama emptied by 90% or more, leaving dense surviving indigenous peasantries anchored in the cool volcanic highlands of Central Mexico, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Guatemala alongside resilient Yucatec Maya parishes [@Lovell1992; @Newson1986; @MacLeod1973]. Simultaneously, across the 99-settlement gazetteer, the decline of 43 pre-Columbian centres and the rise of 56 Spanish-founded administrative cities, silver camps and ports — headed by Puebla de los Ángeles, Antigua Guatemala, Zacatecas, Mérida, Guadalajara and Panamá Viejo — reoriented urban geography toward transatlantic bullion routes and northern mining frontiers, laying the demographic foundation for the slow multi-ethnic recovery that would gather pace after 1650.

# Footnotes

**Note 1 (Tributary-to-Population Conversion Multipliers).** Sixteenth-century New Spain fiscal documents typically record *tributarios* (adult married male taxpayers, with widows and unmarried adults counted as half-tributaries after the 1560s reforms) rather than total souls. Following Cook and Borah [@CookBorah1971] and Gerhard [@Gerhard1993], archival benchmarks in Table \ref{tab:dual-reconciliation} apply conversion factors of 3,3 to 3,5 persons per full tributary for the 1548 to 1550 *Suma de Visitas* (correcting for widespread exemptions of *mayeques*, nobles and service populations) and 2,8 to 3 for post-1565 standardised tributary rolls, supplemented by independent enumerations of non-indigenous *vecinos* (multiplied by 4,5 to 5 persons per Spanish household) and Afro-Mexican residents [@AguirreBeltran1946].

**Note 2 (Dual-Series Divergence at 1518 and Centennial Interpolation at 1650).** Gridded totals in Table \ref{tab:subregion-grid} and Figure \ref{fig:conquest-trajectory} integrate JAGUAR's continuous 5-arc-minute population rasters across exact WGS84 equal-area cell footprints (2.595.905,5 km²), whereas archival benchmarks in Table \ref{tab:dual-reconciliation} reflect regional ethnohistorical reconstructions summed over the same seven *audiencia* masks. The 1518 difference (4,08M gridded versus 18,17M archival) reflects conservative pre-contact scaling in global centennial substrata, while the 1650 gridded uptick (2,99M versus 2,77M archival) reflects log-linear interpolation between the 1600 and 1700 raster frames across the 1620 to 1646 colonial nadir.

**Note 3 (Etymology and Clinical Scope of Cocoliztli).** In classical Nahuatl, *cocoliztli* denotes sickness or pestilence broadly, whereas colonial physicians and chroniclers applied the term specifically to the fulminant febrile-haemorrhagic epidemics of 1545 to 1548 and 1576 to 1581 (*huey cocoliztli*) [@Malanga2020Earth; @AcunaSoto2002]. Ancient genomic identification of *Salmonella enterica* Paratyphi C at Teposcolula-Yucundaa [@Vagene2018] establishes an introduced Eurasian enteric pathogen in the 1545 to 1550 wave without excluding regional co-infection by typhus or drought-amplified haemorrhagic viruses.
